entry.title: Neural Network Teaches Gravity Not to Hide
entry.summary: The authors built a neural network emulator that predicts in fractions of a second how dark matter inhomogeneities change under modified gravity. Previously, such calculations took hours; now they take moments. The emulator was tested on synthetic data and recovered cosmological parameters with high accuracy. This is an important step in preparing for new large-scale sky surveys that will look for deviations from Einstein's theory.

entry.title: The Universe Heats Up on Vortices
entry.summary: In theories of gravity with spacetime torsion, inflation (the ultra-fast expansion of the early Universe) may be driven not by a special field but by the dynamic torsion itself. It naturally couples to Standard Model particles, so the reheating process after inflation proceeds differently. The authors calculated how the inflaton (the particle responsible for inflation) decays and found that particle production via quantum anomalies gives a significant contribution. This sets a lower bound on the reheating temperature and changes our understanding of how the Universe became hot.

entry.title: Dark Matter from Magnetic Droplets
entry.summary: The authors built a model where dark matter consists of magnetic monopoles that formed as the hot universe cooled. Normally, too few such particles are produced, but adding a light dark fermion suppresses its abundance, making monopoles the dominant component. Their mass is about one hundred million gigaelectronvolts, beyond the reach of current detectors. However, the model predicts a distinctive dark radiation and gravitational waves that future observatories might detect.

entry.title: How Orbits Reveal the Universe's Curvature
entry.summary: Scientists compared how almost circular orbits change in classical physics and in general relativity. They derived exact formulas for the perihelion shift—the point of closest approach—and found conditions under which the orbit remains closed. It turns out that even a tiny cosmological constant can affect this shift. The authors also discovered a rare case where the shift disappears entirely.

entry.title: Black Hole Echo: What the Horizon Sounds Like
entry.summary: Physicists are studying the echoes of gravitational waves from exotic compact objects—ghostly stand-ins for black holes. It turns out that the frequency of these reflections isn't constant; instead, they cluster according to a hyperbolic law. This clustering depends only on the external curvature of space, not on the object's internal structure. The discovery offers a new way to peer beyond the event horizon.

entry.title: Three Faces of the Cosmos: Geometry, Growth, and the Beginning
entry.summary: The standard cosmological model ΛCDM (cold dark matter and dark energy) does an excellent job describing most observations, but a few discrepancies have emerged. To stress-test the model, researchers split the influence of three different epochs: the geometry of space, the growth of large-scale structure, and the physics of the early Universe. They found that geometry and the early Universe give different values for the density of matter—a difference of about two standard deviations. Meanwhile, structure growth agrees with both. This could hint at hidden tensions in our understanding of the cosmos.

entry.title: Where Did Matter Come From? A Fresh Look at the Boltzmann Equation
entry.summary: In the first moments after the Big Bang, nearly equal amounts of matter and antimatter should have completely annihilated each other. But a tiny imbalance in favor of matter persisted — otherwise galaxies and stars would never have formed. A new study offers a more rigorous derivation of the Boltzmann equation for this process. The authors included corrections from particle interactions, making the calculation systematic. This brings us closer to understanding how a tiny bit of matter survived and became the visible universe.

entry.title: How Chaos Gives Birth to Life: The Secret Switch
entry.summary: In a computer model of the primordial 'soup', scientists observed how random collisions of molecules give rise to ordered chains. They measured a special property of the mixture—'causal influence', i.e., its ability to influence its own future. When this influence crosses a critical threshold, self-copying molecules spontaneously appear in the soup. By controlling this influence, one can extend or shorten the lifespan of such copiers. The discovery hints at how life might have arisen from chaos—and how it might be controlled.

entry.title: Mosaic on the Surface of a Black Hole
entry.summary: Physicists have proposed a general method for calculating the hidden information in black holes by dividing their surface into tiny identical cells. It turns out this information consists of two parts: the main one, proportional to the area, and a fixed constant correction. This approach relies on minimal assumptions and explains why black holes 'remember' information precisely on the surface. It's a step toward understanding the quantum nature of spacetime.

entry.title: Light Fringes Betray a Photon’s Spin
entry.summary: Two centuries ago, Arago and Fresnel noticed that light waves produce fringes only when they oscillate in the same plane. Now physicists have repeated the experiment with quantum states. They mixed an ordinary laser beam with a single photon, twisted either to the left or to the right. By measuring brightness and polarization, they saw that the fringe pattern depends on the photon’s spin direction. So a way to determine its internal rotation purely optically — just by looking at the picture — was born. The discovery will be useful in quantum networks and cryptography.

entry.title: Gravitational Waves in a Noisy Room
entry.summary: A precise correspondence has been established between the description of weak gravitational waves in an expanding universe and the well-known Caldeira–Leggett model of open systems. This reduces complex equations to one: a generalized Langevin equation for the gravitational wave. The influence of matter is captured by a single function—the spectral density. This approach opens the door to quantizing gravitational perturbations and the stochastic dynamics of spacetime.

entry.title: The Invisible Pattern of Dark Energy Across the Sky
entry.summary: In the 'kinetic gravity braiding' (KGB) model, dark energy and gravity are far more tightly linked than usually assumed. For the first time, the researchers used computer simulations to create full-sky maps for this case. They found that the bending of light and shifts in its frequency can deviate from standard predictions by tens of percent. This means next-generation telescopes will be able to pick up fine details on the sky map that betray dark energy's true nature.

entry.title: Avalanche of Cells: The Critical Edge
entry.summary: Researchers used a cellular automaton—a simplified model where activity propagates between neighboring elements according to random rules. Under certain conditions, the system neither dies out nor grows unchecked, but enters a critical interval. Here, avalanches govern dynamics: small bursts can trigger large ones, but not always. The work shows how spatial patterns of activity, equally complex at any scale, and the unusual statistics of bursts link two regimes—and why this matters for understanding complex systems.

entry.title: Chaos Patterns: A 3D Crystal Made from Liquid Light
entry.summary: In crystals made of exciton-polaritons—particles that blend light and matter—scientists have modeled how chaotic fluctuations coalesce into strict patterns. It turns out these patterns obey the same mathematical laws that govern the growth of mountain slopes, wildfires, or bacterial colonies. The work paves the way to studying non-equilibrium processes in a controlled quantum system, helping us understand how structure emerges from disorder across the natural world.

entry.title: Twisted Crown: How a Magnetic Vortex Rewrites Sunspots
entry.summary: In the Sun's corona, magnetic fields twist and reconnect. Sometimes this reaches the surface — the photosphere. Scientists discovered that after a flare, a twisted loop, as it unwinds, amplifies currents at the base far from the explosion site. Around an old sunspot, a dark scar grows — a region of intensified magnetic field. This discovery explains long-standing mysteries of the Sun and other stars.

entry.title: Mini-brains learn to ignore repeated stimuli
entry.summary: Scientists have developed a method to trace signals in mini-brains—tiny lab-grown replicas of the brain. They found that the response to a stimulus is an almost instantaneous synchronous burst, not a spreading wave. When the stimulus is repeated day after day, the reaction weakens and covers an ever-smaller area. A comparison with a control organoid that was never stimulated proved that this is a result of experience, not just maturation. The work helps to understand how neural networks adapt to external inputs.

entry.title: Invisible clouds around spinning black holes
entry.summary: Scientists explored how a special kind of matter—a scalar field—behaves near black holes. It turns out that when the black hole spins, the field condenses into dense clouds that move in sync with the horizon. As the rotation slows down, the clouds freeze in place and can persist even around a completely stationary black hole. This explains how dark matter can accumulate around such objects.

entry.title: The Quantum Choir: Why an Extra Soloist Doesn't Boost Volume
entry.summary: Physicists studied how local noise and spontaneous emission affect the collective glow of atoms, known as Dicke superradiance. Normally, the brightness of such a glow scales with the square of the number of atoms. A new theory shows that depending on the noise strength, three regimes are possible: fully collective, partially collective, and independent. Under strong noise, even a large number of atoms emit as independent loners.

entry.title: Why the most massive stars aren't the largest
entry.summary: Astronomers have long puzzled over why the heaviest stars in the universe are far from being the largest in size. A new study explains it by a shift from normal mass outflow to a powerful wind, pushed by light pressure. This model precisely reproduces the observed radius boundary—a kink in the graph where stars are compared by luminosity and temperature. Understanding this mechanism will improve predictions of black hole masses and merger rates detected by gravitational-wave observatories, and also help decode the light from distant galaxies.

entry.title: How Two Rhythms Give Birth to a Slow Quantum Wave
entry.summary: Researchers irradiated a cloud of rubidium atoms with two laser beams of slightly different frequencies. Their rhythms combined, giving rise to a long beat period—exactly like in music: two nearly identical notes produce a slow 'wah-wah'. This regime is robust against disturbances and opens the way to controlling time in quantum devices.

entry.title: The Walker Paradox: Why Farther Means Faster
entry.summary: A model of the walking protein kinesin shows that it obeys the Mpemba effect. Even at equilibrium, the motor settles down faster when starting from a more excited state. Neither fuel nor load changes the picture. The anomaly is detectable in its speed — and measurable. This offers a new way to explore the odd behavior of nonequilibrium systems inside cells.

entry.title: Bubbles in the early universe hide gravitational waves
entry.summary: In the first moments after the Big Bang, the universe was like a boiling cauldron: bubbles of a new state of matter appeared and grew everywhere. Now it turns out their motion hits hydrodynamic barriers — as if invisible obstacles arrest growth. Because of this, unexpected shock waves are born inside the bubbles, and the most powerful gravitational waves may simply never arise. The discovery forces a fresh look at the hunt for cosmic ripples.

entry.title: Bright Quasars Hide Magnesium Lines — It's All About Gas Density
entry.summary: For nearly 50 years, astronomers have known: the brighter the quasar, the weaker the magnesium lines in its spectrum. This was dubbed the Baldwin effect, but its cause remained unknown. A new analysis of over 41 thousand quasars revealed that the density of gas in the cloud surrounding the central black hole is the key. The effect is more pronounced in radio-loud quasars, and the crucial parameter is how brightly the quasar shines compared to the theoretical limit. This discovery places the Baldwin effect into the broader picture of galaxy evolution.

entry.title: Current sparks forbidden harmonics
entry.summary: Scientists have found that even harmonics can be produced in symmetric crystals by passing a current through them. The current creates a non-equilibrium state that distorts the electron cloud, breaking the system's symmetry. The brightness of the even harmonics directly depends on the current strength. This turns them into an ultrafast sensor for electrical processes in microelectronics.

entry.title: The Stellar Forge: A First Glimpse at the Birth of Cosmic Crystals
entry.summary: A flare was spotted at the young star EC 53, coinciding with the appearance of characteristic mineral lines of forsterite and enstatite. This confirms that crystals are born in the hot inner disk precisely when the star is devouring material. The same crystals have been found in comets, but how they got there has been a mystery. The answer lies in the outflow structure: a narrow jet and a wider wind carry the dust outward. A similar mechanism may have operated in the young Solar System.

entry.title: PhySR: Physics Helps a Neural Network See Through the Radio Static
entry.summary: Radio telescopes collect incomplete data, so images come out blurred and fine details vanish. PhySR is a neural network that has a physical model of the telescope built right in: how the antenna beam responds to a signal and how it gets smeared during processing. It learns to restore clarity without needing pristine reference images. On data from the future SKA telescope, the method boosted quality severalfold, beating conventional algorithms and other neural nets.

entry.title: Fractions of a Second That Prevent a Blackout
entry.summary: When a fault strikes, the grid’s automated protections have just a split second to isolate the damage. If they're too slow, generators lose sync—and whole cities go dark. A new neural network, ES-PINN, nails down that critical threshold: the instant after which recovery is impossible. It leans on the laws of physics and works faster than traditional brute-force computer simulations. This lets engineers spot grid weaknesses ahead of time, preventing a single fault from cascading into widespread blackouts.

entry.title: Black Holes: Neutrino Factories
entry.summary: Around supermassive black holes, protons crash into X-ray photons at colossal speeds. These collisions give birth to neutrinos, some of the most elusive particles in the universe. Gamma rays from the same process are absorbed by plasma, keeping the source invisible, while neutrinos escape. Data from the IceCube neutrino telescope confirm that this is how nature’s particle factory works, explaining the mysterious background of cosmic neutrinos and rays.

entry.title: Blurred Light from Neutron Stars Reveals Their Spin Rate
Reverse Tides: The Remarkable Deformation of Boson Stars
entry.summary: Boson stars are hypothetical clumps of boson particles that can all pile into the same quantum state. Physicists calculated how such stars deform under tidal forces from a neighboring body. They found that under certain conditions the electric Love numbers (a measure of deformability) can become negative. This means the star does not stretch toward the perturbing object but instead squashes along that axis—like the ocean under the Moon not bulging up but dipping into a trough. The finding will help distinguish boson stars from black holes when observing gravitational waves.

entry.title: The Stellar Conductor of Planetary Atmospheres
entry.summary: This review explores the deep connection between stellar radiation and planetary habitability. The long-term evolution of a star's luminosity and magnetic activity acts as the main driver of atmospheric escape and climate shifts. Chemistry triggered by ultraviolet light and energetic particles can both build the building blocks of life and sterilize a planet's surface. Understanding these mechanisms is critical for selecting targets for future missions and interpreting observed spectra.

entry.title: Dark-Sector Seesaw: How a Scalar Spring Solves Cosmological Puzzles
entry.summary: The standard cosmological model faces two discrepancies: different measurements of the Universe's expansion rate and hints of evolving dark energy. This work explores a model where the mass of dark matter depends on a single field. It is shown that such a field naturally causes an energy injection in the early Universe and creates the appearance of phantom behavior at late times. Both effects are tied to key epochs rather than artificial scales, reducing fine-tuning and alleviating the structure growth problem.

entry.title: Uneven Tunnel Chain: How Gravity Rewrote the History of the Early Universe
entry.summary: The standard chain inflation model predicts a low energy scale and does not produce noticeable gravitational waves. Introducing a natural coupling of the field to spacetime curvature changes the transition rate along the chain. This breaks the rigid correlation and opens a high-energy regime with a scale of ~10¹¹ GeV. The model predicts a varying tilt in the spectrum of inhomogeneities and gravitational waves from bubble collisions at frequencies accessible to future interferometers. Thus, the uneven chain of tunnels becomes testable by multiple methods.

entry.title: Fountain of Debris: Where the Dust Settled After the DART Impact
entry.summary: Numerical simulation of 20 million trajectories showed that the vast majority of debris scattered into space over two years. However, a small part fell back: on the satellite the layer reached 1,5 mm, and on the main asteroid in one area up to 11,5 mm. The direction of the ejecta cone plays a key role: a scenario close to opposing the impact creates a compact patch. These results provide important context for the Hera mission.

entry.title: Contour Map of Stellar Nurseries: Computer Vision Finds Clusters in the Fireworks Galaxy
entry.summary: Here is a map of the galaxy Fireworks Galaxy (NGC 6946), where instead of cities, stellar nurseries are marked. Using archival images from the Edwin Hubble, an algorithm resembling a cartographer outlined the contours of regions where the density of young blue stars is especially high. It discovered 6410 candidates, measured their brightness and sizes. Analysis of star formation in them yielded a power-law slope of about 2.2, challenging old models. The catalog is open and will serve as a testing ground for studying stellar evolution.

entry.title: Gas Curtain of 'Little Red Dots': Why It's So Common in the Early Universe
entry.summary: Astronomers analyzed 40 'little red dots' (LRDs) — distant compact galaxies with active nuclei spotted by JWST. They found that Balmer absorption lines, indicating dense gas, occur 850 times more frequently in these objects than in typical active nuclei. Almost always, this gas is moving away from the black hole, forming a semitransparent veil. This veil likely gives LRDs their mysterious red hue, reprocessing the central source's radiation.

entry.title: Gravitational Rudder: How a Gas Disk Rips Binary Stars Apart in the Galactic Center
entry.summary: In galactic nuclei, gas disks can be so massive that their non-spherical gravitational field creates a powerful torque on stellar orbits. New research shows that this torque drives binary systems to be torn apart by the black hole's tidal forces. One star is captured into a tight orbit, while the other is ejected at enormous speed. For the center of the Milky Way, such a disk, formed about 5 million years ago, triggered a burst of roughly a hundred disruptions. This explains the origin of the hypervelocity star S5-HVS1 and predicts an entire population of yet-unseen faint S-cluster stars.

entry.title: A Tangled Skein: How Two Factors Drive Weather on a Lonely Planet
entry.summary: Schrader and colleagues applied principal component analysis to the continuous JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy of the brown dwarf SIMP 0136. Two components described 79% of the variability—fluctuations in effective temperature and vertical cloud extent. The object's rotation traces a triangular trajectory in component space, indicating a mixture of three extreme states. Comparison with physical models confirms that the same two factors dominate in theory as well.

entry.title: Black Hole Infants: A Handicap Race in the Early Universe
entry.summary: Data from JWST posed a puzzle for astronomers: black holes in the early Universe accumulated billions of solar masses while their galaxies were still assembling. Twelve cosmological simulations from AESOPICA reproduced this handicap race. By varying the weight of the 'seeds' and allowing them to occasionally 'binge' beyond the limit, scientists showed that any runner could become a champion. The key is observational selection: the telescope sees only winners; the peloton remains in shadow.

entry.title: The Dark Side of the Pendulum
entry.summary: Scientists have proposed a model in which dark matter and dark energy periodically exchange energy. This exchange can change direction over time—sometimes from dark matter to dark energy, and sometimes back. The model was tested against observational data—the cosmic microwave background, supernovae, and galaxy distribution. It turns out that such a 'seesaw' energy transfer does not contradict what we see in the universe. Although the new model does not explain the data better than the standard one, it opens the door to more complex interaction scenarios in the dark sector.

entry.title: Tricoupler on a Chip: The Knot That Cancels Starlight
entry.summary: To spot a planet next to a blinding star, astronomers use nulling interferometry—a technique that cancels the star's light via destructive interference. Photonic integrated circuits (PICs) allow this to be done compactly and stably. This study investigates tricouplers—symmetric three-waveguide beam splitters on a silicon platform, inherently capable of an achromatic null. In lab tests, a contrast of up to 4×10⁻⁶ was achieved in monochromatic mode, and ~10⁻³ over a 200 nm band. The limitations stem from the chromaticity of thermo-optic modulators and birefringence, which points the way to further improvements.

entry.title: Imperturbable Corona: How Polarization Revealed the Black Hole's Stable Geometry
entry.summary: In 2022, three observatories — IXPE, NICER, and NuSTAR — simultaneously monitored the famous binary system. They captured moments of sharp brightness drops — dips caused by dense clumps of stellar wind blocking light from the accretion disk. Spectra showed that the soft emission from the disk was absorbed, while the hard emission was not. Polarization measurements surprised: the degree and angle of polarization remained the same as during non-eclipsed times. This indicates that the polarized light originates in an extended, flattened corona that local clouds cannot perturb.

entry.title: Cluster Crucible: Random Forest Identifies Returning Galaxies
entry.summary: The outskirts of massive galaxy clusters are home to both infalling galaxies and 'returners'—objects that have already been through the core. Distinguishing them is tricky, and the mix biases conclusions. A new random forest classifier, trained on 324 simulations, uses observed properties to tell whether a galaxy has been through the crucible. Accuracy reaches 84%, and the threshold is adjustable. Applied to NGC 4254 with its tail, it shows: that galaxy is a newcomer.

entry.title: How to Weigh the Universe Without a Scale
entry.summary: Scientists have devised a way to study the distribution of ordinary matter in the universe using fast radio bursts and galaxy maps. They compared two methods and showed that the new approach yields much more information. With it, one can measure more precisely how matter clumps together, even without knowing the distances to the bursts themselves. This is important because most bursts currently lack known distances, and the situation is unlikely to change dramatically in the future.

entry.title: A Spinning Star Puts Gravity to the Test
entry.summary: Astronomers have studied star S301, which orbits the supermassive black hole at the center of our galaxy. Its orbit is highly elongated—it swoops close to the black hole and then swings far away. At closest approach, gravity warps space so strongly that the star's spin axis should tilt slightly. The scientists calculated how noticeable this tilt would be for telescopes on Earth. If such a shift can be measured, it would provide a new test of Einstein's theory of gravity in a strong field.

entry.title: How to Catch Ghost Neutrinos in the Mountains
entry.summary: Scientists have proposed using mountains as part of a detector for neutrinos—particles that barely interact with matter. A special process, the Glashow resonance, can distinguish antineutrinos from neutrinos. This helps us understand how these particles are born in space. New telescopes TAMBO and TRINITY will be able to measure the ratio of different neutrino types. This approach opens the way to unraveling the sources of the most energetic particles in the universe.

entry.title: How Galactic Bars Change the Dance of Black Holes
entry.summary: When galaxies collide, their central black holes start to approach each other and eventually merge, producing gravitational waves. But real galaxies have stellar bars—elongated clusters of stars—that can alter the pace of this dance. Scientists have created a computer model based on artificial intelligence that quickly predicts how a bar will affect the time it takes for black holes to come together. It turns out that bars can either delay or accelerate their encounter, depending on the conditions. This approach makes it possible for the first time to estimate these timescales for thousands of galaxies from cosmological simulations without spending years of computation.

entry.title: Cosmic Strings: Echoes of the Universe's Birth
entry.summary: Right after the Big Bang, ultra-thin but heavy objects—cosmic strings—could have existed in space. They are like cracks in the fabric of spacetime. New research shows how different types of these strings were born and decayed, creating a distinctive 'ring'—gravitational waves. This signal, though very weak today, could carry unique information about the very first moments of the world and about fundamental string theory.

entry.title: Horizon at the Pass: The Moment the Future Froze
entry.summary: This theoretical work links the mysterious behavior of dark energy to the geometry of spacetime. In it, the phantom divide is not just a number but a point where the horizon stops, like the peak of a mountain pass. The direction of descent depends on the 'dimensionality' of the horizon's entropy. The predictions align with preliminary data from the DESI observatory and can be tested with future observations.

entry.title: Galaxies without dark matter: a sieve for the invisible
entry.summary: Recently discovered galaxies almost devoid of dark matter allow us to test its microscopic properties. The key idea: if dark matter interacted strongly with baryons, it would not separate in collisions. Constraints have been obtained for momentum-transfer cross sections, dissipative models, and ultralight axions. The method complements cosmological tests.
